title: What is the Java Platform Module System (JPMS, Java 9), what directives does `module-info.java` use (requires/exports/opens/provides/uses), and when is adopting it worth the friction?
shortTitle: What is the Java Platform Module System (JPMS), and what do the module-info.java directives do?
keyPoints: JPMS groups packages into named modules declared in module-info.java with explicit dependencies and a defined public surface.
The requires directive names dependencies, requires transitive re-exports them, and requires static makes them compile-time only.
The exports directive makes a package visible to other modules, while a qualified exports restricts visibility to named friends.
The opens directive permits deep reflection into a package at run time, which frameworks like Hibernate and Jackson need.
The provides and uses directives wire ServiceLoader with compiler-checked declarations, replacing META-INF/services text files.
At startup the module system resolves the full dependency graph, so a missing module fails the launch instead of failing hours later.
The jlink tool builds trimmed custom runtimes containing only the modules your application needs, shrinking containers dramatically.

s1_definition.oneliner: JPMS turns a loose bag of packages into named modules with declared dependencies and an explicit public surface, enforced by the compiler and the JVM.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Module** – a named, self-describing group of packages declared in `module-info.java` with explicit dependencies and a defined public surface.
- **requires** – declares a dependency on another module; `requires transitive` re-exports it, `requires static` makes it compile-time only.
- **exports** – makes a package visible to other modules at compile and run time; a qualified `exports ... to` restricts visibility to named modules.
- **opens** – allows deep reflection (`setAccessible(true)`) into a package at run time, required by frameworks like Hibernate and Jackson.
- **provides ... with / uses** – wires the `ServiceLoader` mechanism with compiler-checked declarations replacing META-INF/services files.
- **Strong encapsulation** – public classes in non-exported packages are invisible to other modules, which is the headline benefit of JPMS.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India as a secure building. Before JPMS, every department's doors were unlocked and anyone could walk into the vault, the audit room, or HR and grab internal files as long as they knew the room name. JPMS is like issuing each department a signed charter that says which other departments it needs (requires), which of its own rooms the public may enter (exports), and which rooms the auditors may inspect with a special pass (opens). If the payments department says it needs the fraud department but the fraud department does not exist, the building manager refuses to open in the morning instead of discovering the problem at noon when a customer is waiting.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                  module-info.java                     │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  requires com.bank.audit           (dependency)      │
  │  requires transitive com.bank.model (re-exported)    │
  │  exports com.bank.transfer.api     (public surface)  │
  │  opens com.bank.transfer.entity    (reflection)      │
  │  provides FeeCalculator with Gst.. (service)         │
  │  uses AuditSink                    (service consumer)│
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Module Graph at Startup:
  ┌──────────────┐    requires    ┌──────────────┐
  │ com.bank.app │───────────────▶│com.bank.     │
  │              │                │  transfer    │
  └──────────────┘                └──────┬───────┘
                                         │ requires
                                         ▼
                                  ┌──────────────┐
                                  │ com.bank.    │
                                  │   audit      │
                                  └──────┬───────┘
                                         │ requires
                                         ▼
                                  ┌──────────────┐
                                  │  java.base   │
                                  │ (always      │
                                  │  present)    │
                                  └──────────────┘

  Encapsulation:
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  module com.bank.transfer             │
  │                                       │
  │  ┌─────────────────────┐  EXPORTED    │
  │  │ com.bank.transfer   │◀── other     │
  │  │        .api         │    modules   │
  │  └─────────────────────┘    can see   │
  │                                       │
  │  ┌─────────────────────┐  OPENED      │
  │  │ com.bank.transfer   │◀── Hibernate │
  │  │      .entity        │    can       │
  │  └─────────────────────┘    reflect   │
  │                                       │
  │  ┌─────────────────────┐  HIDDEN      │
  │  │ com.bank.transfer   │  ✗ nobody    │
  │  │     .internal       │    can see   │
  │  └─────────────────────┘              │
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The Java Platform Module System, added in Java 9 under Project Jigsaw, is a layer above packages that groups them into named modules, each described by a module-info.java file. A module declares what it depends on with requires, what packages it makes public with exports, which packages are open for deep reflection with opens, and how it participates in the service loader mechanism with provides and uses. The two big wins are strong encapsulation, meaning a public class in a non-exported package is invisible to other modules, and reliable configuration, meaning the module graph is resolved and validated at startup so a missing dependency fails the launch instead of failing hours later in production.

In the banking work at National Bank of India the problem that modules solve directly was a shared payments library. On the old classpath, other teams reached into internal helper classes because public meant public to everyone, and when the team tried to refactor those helpers the whole bank broke. With modules Rajesh exports only the api package that holds the TransferService, keeps the internal validator package encapsulated so nobody outside can even see it, and is finally free to refactor internals safely. When the reporting team genuinely needed one internal class, Pankaj used a qualified export that reveals that package to the reporting module alone, and when Jackson needed to serialize the account model he used opens on just the model package so the framework can reflect while ordinary code still cannot.

The friction is real and worth acknowledging. Reflective frameworks force you to open many packages, some older libraries are not modular and have to be treated as automatic modules, and the split-package rule can break assemblies that worked fine on the classpath. For a shared library or platform where you want a small enforced public surface and a trimmed jlink runtime, modules are clearly worth it. For an ordinary Spring Boot microservice that runs as a fat JAR on the classpath, the cost usually outweighs the benefit.

Remember one sentence: JPMS turns a loose bag of packages into named modules with declared dependencies and an enforced public surface, so internal code stays hidden and missing dependencies fail at startup instead of in production.
